notes.text: The brothers are using a common expression of their culture to express their horror at being accused of stealing from Joseph. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation.

The phrase **go up** refers to the fact that the land of Canaan was higher in elevation than the country of Egypt. Some translations leave **up** implied. or [As for the rest of you, you may go back home to your father without any trouble]
Compare how you translated the idiom “his anger burned” in Genesis 39:19.

The verb “bring … down” refers to the fact that Egypt was lower in elevation than the region of Canaan. Some translations leave **down** implied. or [to bring our youngest brother here to you so that you can see him for yourself]
The pronoun **us** is inclusive here because what Judah’s father (Jacob) had said included the brothers whom he was talking to.
The phrase **the man’s face** refers to the governor (Joseph) himself. Translate this in a way that is natural in your language. or [The man who sells grain there will not permit us to see him again]

notes.topic: or [and if anything bad happens to him]
notes.text: or [and if anything bad happens to him]
or [you will cause me, your elderly father, so much sorrow that I will die and go down]
This idiom reflects how close the relationship was between Judah’s father and youngest brother. Consider what is the best way to say this in your language.

Throughout this chapter, the same Hebrew word is translated as **slave** when the context has negative connotations (verses 9–10, 16–17, 33), but is translated as **servant** when the context has more positive connotations (verses 7, 9, 16, 18–19, 21, 23–24, 27, 30–32). Do what is best in your language in each context. or [and be your servant]
Judah is speaking of **misery** as if it were a living thing that could **find** his **father**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly.
